42 passing, typecheck clean. Now the refactor evaluation.

**Naming evaluation (first priority).**

`basePremiumOfType` — the name says "the base premium of this type". It now also enforces that the type is insurable at all. Is that a different job? I don't think so: a type MHPCO does not insure has no base premium, and "there is no such thing" is the honest answer to the question the name asks. A rename to `requireBasePremiumOfType` or `lookUpBasePremium` would advertise the throw at every one of its two call sites, where the throw is not what the caller is interested in. The name still fits. No rename.

`BASE_PREMIUM_BY_TYPE` and `INSURANCE_VALUE_BY_TYPE` are both keyed by item type and both currently `Record<string, number>` — and one is now guarded and the other deliberately is not. That asymmetry is real and the prompt tells me not to close it. Leaving it.

**On the error shape.** Four more error cases are coming, and three of them (item not in policy, unknown type on a damage entry, more damages than insured) are claim-side, not quote-side. I have exactly one error today. Any shape I invent now — an error-code enum, a `ClaimOfficeError` subclass, a `requireDefined` helper — would be designed against errors I have only read a one-line description of. The message format `Unknown item type: ${type}` is the only commitment made so far, and it is cheap to revise when the second case tells me whether the cases share a format. Under-abstracting: one inline `throw` stays inline. No error infrastructure.

That leaves the actual improvement. Looking at `basePremiumOfType`:

The function body reads fine, but its doc comment no longer tells the whole story — it promises a number and says nothing about the throw. That is a Rule 2 gap: the comment is now the least accurate line in the function. And there is a genuine behavioural hole sitting next to it that the tests *do* reach.

`groupBasePremium` short-circuits on `count === BLOCK_SIZE` and returns `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` **without ever calling `basePremiumOfType`**. So a policy of exactly three broomsticks prices at 60 G instead of throwing. The guard I was handed only fires on the non-block path. Let me confirm that against the real code rather than assume it.

42 passing, 8 todo, typecheck clean.

## Refactor summary

**Applied:** one Rule 2 (reveals intent) change to the doc comment on `basePremiumOfType` in `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-14_17-35-07_claim-office-example-mapping_exact-hybrid-v2.4-lab-split-cc_opus-5-requesty-no-thinking/src/claim-office.ts`. No executable code changed, so APP mass is unchanged (the function's body is 2 constants + 2 bindings + 1 conditional + 1 invocation = 11 before and after). Mass was not the lever here; the comment was the least accurate line in the function, promising a plain number and not mentioning the throw.

**On the error shape — your judgement call.** I left the single inline `throw` exactly as it is. Three of the four upcoming error cases are claim-side, not quote-side, and I have only one-line descriptions of them. Any shape chosen now (error subclass, code enum, a `requireDefined` helper) would be designed against errors I cannot yet see the format of. The only commitment made so far is the message string, which is cheap to revise once the second case shows whether the cases share a format. Agreed on under-abstracting.

**A correction worth flagging.** I initially read `groupBasePremium` as a hole: it returns `BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` on `count === BLOCK_SIZE` without calling `basePremiumOfType`, which looks like three broomsticks pricing at 60 G instead of throwing. I probed it before changing anything, and it throws correctly. The reason is `calculateItemSurcharges`, which calls `basePremiumOfType(item.type)` per item regardless of block pricing, so every type gets validated on the surcharge path.

The part I'd keep an eye on: that coverage is **incidental**. The unknown-type guard fires for complete blocks only because the surcharge pass happens to touch every item individually. If a future refactor short-circuits the surcharge pass (e.g. skipping items with no `cursed`/`enchantment` fields — plausible, since runes and moonstones carry neither), a complete block of an unknown type would start pricing at 60 G instead of throwing, and no active test would catch it. I did not add a defensive lookup, since no test forces one and that would be implementing ahead. I documented the dependency in the comment instead. A `it("quote with three broomsticks → error")` test case would pin it properly if you want it on the list.

I touched none of the listed deliberate gaps (`insuranceSum` guard, non-null assertions, negative-amount check, damage-count check, dragon-material branch, block-discount scoping).
